claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels (Naᵥ) are membrane proteins which open to facilitate the inward flux of sodium ions into excitable cells.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channels (Naᵥ) are membrane proteins which open to facilitate the inward flux of sodium ions into excitable cells.
evidence: This is a fundamental description of Naᵥ channel function, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In response to stimuli, Naᵥ channels transition from the resting, closed state to an open, conductive state, before rapidly inactivating.
source: In response to stimuli, Naᵥ channels transition from the resting, closed state to an open, conductive state, before rapidly inactivating.
evidence: This describes the well-established functional cycle of Naᵥ channels, representing consensus knowledge in the field.

claim: Dysregulation of the Naᵥ functional cycle due to mutations causes diseases including epilepsy, pain conditions, and cardiac disorders.
source: Dysregulation of this functional cycle due to mutations causes diseases including epilepsy, pain conditions, and cardiac disorders, making Naᵥ channels a significant pharmacological target.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about Naᵥ channelopathies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 decreases Naᵥ1.4 activity by increasing the difficulty of channel opening.
source: The phosphoinositide PI(4,5)P2 decreases Naᵥ1.4 activity by increasing the difficulty of channel opening, accelerating fast inactivation and slowing recovery from fast inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work (Gada et al., 2023) as indicated in the manuscript.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 accelerates fast inactivation of Naᵥ1.4.
source: The phosphoinositide PI(4,5)P2 decreases Naᵥ1.4 activity by increasing the difficulty of channel opening, accelerating fast inactivation and slowing recovery from fast inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work (Gada et al., 2023).

claim: PI(4,5)P2 slows recovery from fast inactivation of Naᵥ1.4.
source: The phosphoinositide PI(4,5)P2 decreases Naᵥ1.4 activity by increasing the difficulty of channel opening, accelerating fast inactivation and slowing recovery from fast inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work (Gada et al., 2023).

claim: PI(4,5)P2 binds stably to inactivated Naᵥ at a conserved site within the DIV S4–S5 linker.
source: Using multiscale molecular dynamics simulations, we show that PI(4,5)P2 binds stably to inactivated Naᵥ at a conserved site within the DIV S4–S5 linker, which couples the voltage-sensing domain (VSD) to the pore.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the multiscale MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The DIV S4–S5 linker couples the voltage-sensing domain (VSD) to the pore.
source: Using multiscale molecular dynamics simulations, we show that PI(4,5)P2 binds stably to inactivated Naᵥ at a conserved site within the DIV S4–S5 linker, which couples the voltage-sensing domain (VSD) to the pore.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Naᵥ channel architecture.

claim: The Naᵥ C-terminal domain is proposed to bind at the DIV S4–S5 linker during recovery from inactivation.
source: As the Naᵥ C-terminal domain is proposed to also bind here during recovery from inactivation, we hypothesize that PI(4,5)P2 prolongs inactivation by competitively binding to this site.
evidence: This is based on prior structural and functional studies, particularly Clairfeuille et al., 2019, cited in the manuscript.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 prolongs inactivation by competitively binding to the DIV S4–S5 linker site.
source: As the Naᵥ C-terminal domain is proposed to also bind here during recovery from inactivation, we hypothesize that PI(4,5)P2 prolongs inactivation by competitively binding to this site.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their simulation data and prior knowledge about CTD binding.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 reduces the mobility of the DIV S4–S5 linker in atomistic simulations.
source: In atomistic simulations, PI(4,5)P2 reduces the mobility of both the DIV S4–S5 linker and the DIII–IV linker, responsible for fast inactivation, slowing the conformational changes required for the channel to recover to the resting state.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RMSF analysis from atomistic simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 reduces the mobility of the DIII–IV linker in atomistic simulations.
source: In atomistic simulations, PI(4,5)P2 reduces the mobility of both the DIV S4–S5 linker and the DIII–IV linker, responsible for fast inactivation, slowing the conformational changes required for the channel to recover to the resting state.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RMSF analysis from atomistic simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The DIII–IV linker is responsible for fast inactivation.
source: In atomistic simulations, PI(4,5)P2 reduces the mobility of both the DIV S4–S5 linker and the DIII–IV linker, responsible for fast inactivation, slowing the conformational changes required for the channel to recover to the resting state.
evidence: This is well-established knowledge about the mechanism of fast inactivation in Naᵥ channels.

claim: In a resting state Naᵥ model, phosphoinositides bind to VSD gating charges.
source: We further show that in a resting state Naᵥ model, phosphoinositides bind to VSD gating charges, which may anchor them and impede VSD activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by coarse-grained simulation data of the resting state model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphoinositide binding to VSD gating charges may anchor them and impede VSD activation.
source: We further show that in a resting state Naᵥ model, phosphoinositides bind to VSD gating charges, which may anchor them and impede VSD activation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the simulation data showing PIP binding to gating charges.

claim: The mammalian Naᵥ channel family consists of nine subtypes (Naᵥ1.1–1.9).
source: In mammals, the Naᵥ channel family consists of nine subtypes (Naᵥ1.1–1.9), distributed throughout the central and peripheral nervous system, as well as in cardiac and skeletal muscle (Yu and Catterall, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Yu and Catterall, 2003.

claim: The Naᵥ1.4 subtype is predominantly expressed in skeletal myofibers.
source: The Naᵥ1.4 subtype is predominantly expressed in skeletal myofibers, where it initiates muscle contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Naᵥ1.4 tissue distribution and function.

claim: Naᵥ1.4 initiates muscle contraction.
source: The Naᵥ1.4 subtype is predominantly expressed in skeletal myofibers, where it initiates muscle contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Naᵥ1.4 physiological function.

claim: Genetic mutations in Naᵥ1.4 are associated with hyperkalemic and hypokalemic periodic paralyses.
source: Genetic mutations in this subtype are associated with various motor dysfunctions, such as both hyperkalemic and hypokalemic periodic paralyses (Mantegazza et al., 2021; Venance et al., 2006; Jurkat-Rott et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mantegazza et al., 2021; Venance et al., 2006; Jurkat-Rott et al., 2000.

claim: Naᵥ1.7 is found in peripheral sensory neurons and is responsible for nociception.
source: Naᵥ1.7 is found in peripheral sensory neurons and is responsible for nociception.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Naᵥ1.7 tissue distribution and function.

claim: Inherited erythromelalgia and small fiber neuropathy arise from gain-of-function Naᵥ1.7 mutations.
source: Several pain disorders, such as inherited erythromelalgia and small fiber neuropathy arise from gain-of-function Naᵥ1.7 mutations (Dib-Hajj et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dib-Hajj et al., 2013.

claim: Naᵥ channels consist of four homologous domains (DI–DIV) arranged in a domain-swapped configuration.
source: Structurally, Naᵥ channels consist of four homologous domains (DI–DIV) arranged in a domain-swapped configuration (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Naᵥ channels, also illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Each domain of Naᵥ channels comprises six transmembrane helices (S1–S6).
source: Each domain comprises six transmembrane helices (S1–S6).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Naᵥ channel architecture.

claim: The central pore domain of Naᵥ channels is formed by S5, S6 helices and selectivity filter.
source: The central pore domain is formed by S5, S6 helices and selectivity filter (SF), while the four peripheral VSDs are formed by S1–S4 (de Lera Ruiz and Kraus, 2015; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations to de Lera Ruiz and Kraus, 2015; Pan et al., 2018.

claim: The four peripheral VSDs of Naᵥ channels are formed by S1–S4.
source: The central pore domain is formed by S5, S6 helices and selectivity filter (SF), while the four peripheral VSDs are formed by S1–S4 (de Lera Ruiz and Kraus, 2015; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations to de Lera Ruiz and Kraus, 2015; Pan et al., 2018.

claim: The pore domain of Naᵥ channels features lateral fenestrations that provide a pathway for the access of small molecules to the pore via the membrane.
source: The pore domain also features lateral fenestrations that provide a pathway for the access of small molecules to the pore via the membrane (Gamal El-Din et al., 2018) and have been shown in computational studies to be accessible to lipid tails (Raju et al., 2013; Boiteux et al., 2014; Martin and Corry, 2014; Tao and Corry, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gamal El-Din et al., 2018.

claim: Lateral fenestrations in Naᵥ channels have been shown in computational studies to be accessible to lipid tails.
source: The pore domain also features lateral fenestrations that provide a pathway for the access of small molecules to the pore via the membrane (Gamal El-Din et al., 2018) and have been shown in computational studies to be accessible to lipid tails (Raju et al., 2013; Boiteux et al., 2014; Martin and Corry, 2014; Tao and Corry, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raju et al., 2013; Boiteux et al., 2014; Martin and Corry, 2014; Tao and Corry, 2022.

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) extends from the DIV S6 helix into the cytoplasm.
source: Additionally, the C-terminal domain (CTD) extends from the DIV S6 helix into the cytoplasm, where it is thought to associate with the DIII–IV and DIV S4–S5 linkers in the resting state (Clairfeuille et al., 2019).
evidence: This is structural knowledge supported by citation to Clairfeuille et al., 2019.

claim: The CTD is thought to associate with the DIII–IV and DIV S4–S5 linkers in the resting state.
source: Additionally, the C-terminal domain (CTD) extends from the DIV S6 helix into the cytoplasm, where it is thought to associate with the DIII–IV and DIV S4–S5 linkers in the resting state (Clairfeuille et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Clairfeuille et al., 2019.

claim: In the resting state, the pore is closed and VSD S4 helices are in the down, deactivated state.
source: In the resting state, the pore is closed and VSD S4 helices are in the down, deactivated state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the resting state conformation of Naᵥ channels.

claim: Membrane depolarization triggers the asynchronous transition of VSD I–III S4 helices to the up, activated conformation, causing Naᵥ channels to open.
source: Membrane depolarization triggers the asynchronous transition of VSD I–III S4 helices to the up, activated conformation, causing Naᵥ channels to open (Cha et al., 1999; Capes et al., 2013; Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cha et al., 1999; Capes et al., 2013; Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2013.

claim: During prolonged depolarization, VSD-IV moves upward, causing the channels to adopt a fast-inactivated state.
source: During prolonged depolarization, VSD-IV moves upward, causing the channels to adopt a fast-inactivated state in which a three-residue Ile-Phe-Met (IFM) hydrophobic motif located on the intracellular linker between DIII and DIV (DIII–IV linker) allosterically closes the pore (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: In the fast-inactivated state, the IFM motif allosterically closes the pore.
source: During prolonged depolarization, VSD-IV moves upward, causing the channels to adopt a fast-inactivated state in which a three-residue Ile-Phe-Met (IFM) hydrophobic motif located on the intracellular linker between DIII and DIV (DIII–IV linker) allosterically closes the pore (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: The CTD is proposed to bind at the S4–S5 linker of VSD-IV and sequester the DIII-IV linker during the resting state.
source: The CTD is proposed to bind at the S4–S5 linker of VSD-IV and sequester the DIII-IV linker during the resting state.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional studies, particularly Clairfeuille et al., 2019.

claim: During fast inactivation, the CTD dissociates from VSD-IV and releases the DIII–IV linker to allow IFM binding.
source: During fast inactivation, the CTD dissociates from VSD-IV and releases the DIII–IV linker to allow IFM binding (Clairfeuille et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Clairfeuille et al., 2019.

claim: Upon repolarization, the VSDs deactivate, the IFM motif disassociates, the CTD rebinds to VSD-IV, and the pore returns to the resting state.
source: Upon repolarization, the VSDs deactivate, the IFM motif disassociates, the CTD rebinds to VSD-IV, and the pore returns to the resting state.
evidence: This describes the established recovery mechanism of Naᵥ channels.

claim: Phosphoinositides (PIPs) are important cellular signaling molecules found on the cytoplasmic leaflet of the mammalian cell membrane.
source: Phosphoinositides (PIPs) are important cellular signaling molecules found on the cytoplasmic leaflet of the mammalian cell membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PIP localization and function.

claim: PIPs can exist in seven forms, with phosphorylation possible at one (PIP1), two (PIP2), or all three (PIP3) positions on the inositol ring.
source: They can exist in seven forms, with phosphorylation possible at one (PIP1), two (PIP2), or all three (PIP3) positions on the inositol ring, at the 3', 4', and/or 5' carbons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PIP chemistry and diversity.

claim: PIPs, particularly PI(4,5)P2, are known to bind and modulate the activity of numerous ion channel families.
source: PIPs, particularly PI(4,5)P2, featuring phosphates at the 4' and 5' carbon positions (Figure 1D), are known to bind and modulate the activity of numerous ion channel families (Hille et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hille et al., 2015.

claim: Some voltage-gated ion channels have been resolved with PI(4,5)P2 bound.
source: These include voltage-gated ion channels, some of which have been resolved with PI(4,5)P2 bound (Sun and MacKinnon, 2020; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sun and MacKinnon, 2020; Gao et al., 2021.

claim: PIP is known to interact with the VSDs of different potassium channels, to stabilize the positive gating charges and support the voltage-sensing mechanism.
source: PIP is known to interact with the VSDs of different potassium channels, to stabilize the positive gating charges and support the voltage-sensing mechanism (Schmidt et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2006.

claim: PIP is proposed to facilitate coupling of VSD movement to pore opening in channels such as Kᵥ7.1 by binding at the VSD-pore interface.
source: By also binding at the VSD-pore interface in channels such as Kᵥ7.1, PIP is proposed to facilitate coupling of VSD movement to pore opening (Sun and MacKinnon, 2020; Kasimova et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sun and MacKinnon, 2020; Kasimova et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2022.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 forms specific interactions with VSD-II of Caᵥ2.2 in the down state, making channel activation more difficult.
source: PI(4,5)P2 also forms specific interactions with VSD-II of Caᵥ2.2 in the down state, making channel activation more difficult (Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2021.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 inhibits Naᵥ1.4 by causing a depolarizing shift in voltage dependence of activation.
source: PI(4,5)P2 inhibits Naᵥ1.4 by causing a depolarizing shift in voltage dependence of activation, accelerating transition to the inactivated state and slowing recovery from inactivation, resulting in reduced peak current and suppression of late current (summarized in Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gada et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 accelerates transition to the inactivated state in Naᵥ1.4.
source: PI(4,5)P2 inhibits Naᵥ1.4 by causing a depolarizing shift in voltage dependence of activation, accelerating transition to the inactivated state and slowing recovery from inactivation, resulting in reduced peak current and suppression of late current (summarized in Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gada et al., 2023.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 slows recovery from inactivation in Naᵥ1.4, resulting in reduced peak current and suppression of late current.
source: PI(4,5)P2 inhibits Naᵥ1.4 by causing a depolarizing shift in voltage dependence of activation, accelerating transition to the inactivated state and slowing recovery from inactivation, resulting in reduced peak current and suppression of late current (summarized in Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gada et al., 2023.

claim: Coarse-grained simulations of Naᵥ1.4 embedded in a complex mammalian membrane showed that glycosphingolipid, PIP, and diacylglycerol (DG) were highly enriched around Naᵥ1.4.
source: Glycosphingolipid, PIP, and diacylglycerol (DG) were highly enriched around Naᵥ1.4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Modest enrichment of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidylserine (PS), and phosphatidylethanolamine was observed around Naᵥ1.4.
source: Additionally, we observed modest enrichment of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidylserine (PS), and phosphatidylethanolamine, and slight depletion of ceramide, sphingomyelin, phosphatidylcholine, and cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the simulation data.

claim: Slight depletion of ceramide, sphingomyelin, phosphatidylcholine, and cholesterol was observed around Naᵥ1.4.
source: Additionally, we observed modest enrichment of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidylserine (PS), and phosphatidylethanolamine, and slight depletion of ceramide, sphingomyelin, phosphatidylcholine, and cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the simulation data.

claim: DG lipids form significant interactions within the lateral fenestrations of Naᵥ1.4.
source: DG lipids form significant interactions within the lateral fenestrations of Naᵥ1.4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PIPs are highly enriched around Naᵥ1.4, particularly near the DIII–IV linker and the VSD-IV.
source: Despite the very low concentration of PIPs (0.5% each of PIP1, PIP2, and PIP3) in the mammalian membrane, they are highly enriched around Naᵥ1.4, particularly near the DIII–IV linker and the VSD-IV (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Contact analysis revealed a putative PIP binding site involving the K1330 residue of the DIII–IV linker and residues R1463, K1466, and R1469 in the DIV S4–S5 linker.
source: Contact analysis revealed a putative PIP binding site involving the K1330 residue of the DIII–IV linker and residues R1463, K1466, and R1469 in the DIV S4–S5 linker, which connects the pore and VSD-IV (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by contact analysis from the simulation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only residues within the identified PIP binding site were occupied by PIPs for more than 80% of simulation time on average.
source: Across all three replicates, only residues within this site were occupied by PIPs for more than 80% (quartile 3+1.5×interquartile range) of simulation time on average (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by occupancy analysis from the simulation data.

claim: The identified PIP binding site residues have higher occupancies for PIP compared to other lipids, including other negatively charged phospholipids (PA, PS, and PI).
source: We note that these residues have higher occupancies for PIP compared to other lipids, including other negatively charged phospholipids (PA, PS, and PI) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by comparative occupancy analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All three PIP species bind at the identified site on VSD-IV and DIII–IV linker in enriched PIP simulations.
source: Across 10 replicates of these enriched PIP simulations, each carried out for 80 µs, we observed all three PIP species binding at the identified site on VSD-IV and DIII–IV linker (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the enriched PIP simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PIP1 only forms stable interactions when it approaches and binds from the VSD-I side.
source: PIPs can approach and bind to this site from either side of the VSD, however, PIP1 only forms stable interactions when it approaches and binds from the VSD-I side while PIP2 and PIP3 usually bind from the VSD-III side (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of binding trajectories in the simulation data.

claim: PIP2 and PIP3 usually bind from the VSD-III side.
source: PIPs can approach and bind to this site from either side of the VSD, however, PIP1 only forms stable interactions when it approaches and binds from the VSD-I side while PIP2 and PIP3 usually bind from the VSD-III side (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of binding trajectories in the simulation data.

claim: Additional positively charged residues in the DIII–IV linker (K1329, K1333, and K1352) and DIV S4 (R1460) support PIP binding.
source: These enriched PIP simulations also revealed additional positively charged residues in the DIII–IV linker (K1329, K1333, and K1352) and DIV S4 (R1460) which support binding.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the enriched PIP simulation data.

claim: There were 156 PIP binding/unbinding events with duration greater than 2 µs occurring in the identified site.
source: There were 156 PIP binding/unbinding events with duration greater than 2 µs occurring in the identified site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by binding event analysis from the simulation data.

claim: Of the 156 PIP binding events, 43 were with PIP1, 44 with PIP2, and 33 with PIP3.
source: Of these, 43 were with PIP1, 44 with PIP2, and 33 with PIP3.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by binding event analysis from the simulation data.

claim: The number of short-term (2–10 µs) PIP interactions decreased with headgroup charge.
source: The number of short-term (2–10 µs) interactions decreased with headgroup charge.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of binding duration distributions from the simulation data.

claim: PIP1 formed the greatest number of short-term interactions while PIP3 had the fewest.
source: That is, PIP1 formed the greatest number of short-term interactions while PIP3 had the fewest.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of binding duration distributions from the simulation data.

claim: Of the 31 binding events with duration greater than 10 µs, 7 were with PIP1, 15 with PIP2, and 9 with PIP3.
source: Of the 31 binding events with duration greater than 10 µs, 7 were with PIP1, 15 with PIP2, and 9 with PIP3 (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by binding event analysis from the simulation data.

claim: PIP1 binding is most frequently coordinated by two positive charges in VSD-IV and zero or one residue in the DIII–IV linker.
source: PIP1 (headgroup charge: –3e) binding is most frequently coordinated by two positive charges in VSD-IV and zero or one residue in the DIII–IV linker.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from the simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PIP2 binding most frequently involves one or two interactions from the DIII–IV linker and three from VSD-IV for a total of five interactions.
source: PIP2 (headgroup charge: –5e) binding most frequently involves one or two interactions from the DIII–IV linker and three from VSD-IV for a total of five interactions.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from the simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Despite its greater negative charge, PIP3 interacts similarly to PIP1, and has fewer interactions than PIP2.
source: Interestingly, despite its greater negative charge, PIP3 (headgroup charge: –7e) interacts similarly to PIP1, and has fewer interactions than PIP2.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from the simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In silico mutation of the eight residues implicated in PIP binding to leucine or glutamate significantly reduced PIP binding.
source: In silico mutation of the eight residues implicated in PIP binding to leucine (charge neutralization while preserving side chain size) or glutamate (charge reversal) significantly reduced PIP binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by mutant simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The PI(4,5)P2 headgroup was stable at the binding site identified in coarse-grained simulations (RMSD <2.2 Å).
source: In these simulations, the PI(4,5)P2 headgroup was stable at the binding site identified in coarse-grained simulations (root mean square deviation [RMSD] <2.2 Å) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RMSD analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 binding is predominantly coordinated by R1469 on the DIV S4–S5 linker, as well as R1466 and R1463.
source: PI(4,5)P2 binding is predominantly coordinated by R1469 on the DIV S4–S5 linker, as well as R1466 and R1463.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: The PI(4,5)P2 headgroup forms electrostatic interactions with K1329 and K1330 in the DIII–IV linker.
source: The PI(4,5)P2 headgroup also forms electrostatic interactions with K1329 and K1330 in the DIII–IV linker, but forms few contacts with K1333 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from atomistic simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 4'-phosphate of PI(4,5)P2 formed interactions with residues belonging to the DIII–IV linker (K1329 and K1333) and DIV S4–S5 linker (K1666 and R1469) with similar frequency, in 55–60% of simulation frames.
source: The 4'-phosphate formed interactions with residues belonging to the DIII–IV linker (K1329 and K1333) and DIV S4–S5 linker (K1666 and R1469) with similar frequency, in 55–60% of simulation frames (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction frequency analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: The 5'-phosphate of PI(4,5)P2 formed contacts with three VSD-IV S4–S5 residues (R1463, K1466, and R1469) in 70–98% of simulation frames and DIII–IV linker residues in 37–48% of frames.
source: In contrast, the 5'-phosphate formed contacts with three VSD-IV S4–S5 residues (R1463, K1466, and R1469) in 70–98% of simulation frames and DIII–IV linker residues in 37–48% of frames.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction frequency analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: The 5'-phosphate is more important for coordinating VSD-IV S4–S5 residues while the 4'-phosphate associates with both regions of the binding site.
source: Taken together, this data suggests that although the headgroup is flexible when bound, the 5'-phosphate is more important for coordinating VSD-IV S4–S5 residues while the 4'-phosphate associates with both regions of the binding site.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the interaction frequency data from atomistic simulations.

claim: PI(4)P bound from the VSD-III side is a stable pose (RMSD <2 Å).
source: Atomistic simulations of PI(4)P bound from the VSD-III side show that this is also a stable pose (RMSD <2 Å), where the headgroup interacts with the same positively charged residues as seen for PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RMSD analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: The residues on the S4–S5 linker, R1463, K1466, and R1469, predominantly bind to the 4'-phosphate of PI(4)P.
source: The residues on the S4–S5 linker, R1463, K1466, and R1469, predominantly bind to the 4'-phosphate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: Residues P1336 and R1337 in the DIII–IV linker downstream of the IFM motif are significantly less mobile with PI(4,5)P2 present.
source: Although the DIII–IV linker remains bound throughout simulations both with and without PIPs, residues P1336 and R1337 in the DIII–IV linker downstream of the IFM motif are significantly less mobile with PI(4,5)P2 present (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RMSF analysis from atomistic simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Seven residues belonging to the DIV S4–S5 linker, including binding residues K1466 and R1469, have significantly lower mobility when PI(4,5)P2 is bound.
source: Additionally, seven residues belonging to the DIV S4–S5 linker, including binding residues K1466 and R1469, also have significantly lower mobility when PI(4,5)P2 is bound (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RMSF analysis from atomistic simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In simulations of WT Naᵥ1.4, the IFM has a reduced stability within its binding pocket when PIP is excluded from the membrane.
source: In simulations of WT Naᵥ1.4, the IFM has a reduced stability within its binding pocket when PIP is excluded from the membrane (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by distance analysis from coarse-grained simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The IQM motif has a greater probability of being tightly associated with the receptor pocket in the presence of PIP compared to without it.
source: We find that the IQM motif has a greater probability of being tightly associated with the receptor pocket in the presence of PIP compared to without it (Figure 4E), supporting our observation that PIP can stabilize the channel in the inactivated state.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by distance distribution analysis from coarse-grained simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The presence of PIP may partially rescue some of the structural defects associated with inactivation dysfunction in Naᵥ mutants.
source: This suggests that the presence of PIP may partially rescue some of the structural defects associated with inactivation dysfunction in Naᵥ mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the IQM mutant simulation data.

claim: The PIP binding poses seen in simulations are similar to resolved binding poses for PI(4,5)P2 in cryo-EM structures of Caᵥ2.2 and Kᵥ7.1.
source: The PIP binding poses seen in our simulations are similar to resolved binding poses for PI(4,5)P2 in cryo-EM structures of Caᵥ2.2 and Kᵥ7.1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There are more positively charged residues present in the S4/S4–S5 linker regions of DIV compared to the other domains in Naᵥ1.4.
source: A sequence alignment of Naᵥ1.4 VSDs shows that there are more positively charged residues present in the S4/S4–S5 linker regions of DIV compared to the other domains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The high sequence similarity in the S4/S5–S5 linker and DIII–IV linker regions between the nine human Naᵥ channel subtypes suggests conservation of the PIP binding site.
source: Additionally, the high sequence similarity in the S4/S5–S5 linker and DIII–IV linker regions between the nine human Naᵥ channel subtypes suggests conservation of the PIP binding site (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PIPs bind to the analogous site in inactivated Naᵥ1.7 structure, interacting with residues belonging to both the DIII–IV linker and VSD-IV for durations comparable to Naᵥ1.4.
source: In triplicate 50 µs coarse-grained simulations, PIPs bind to the analogous site to that seen in inactivated Naᵥ1.4 in the inactivated Naᵥ1.7 structure, interacting with residues belonging to both the DIII–IV linker and VSD-IV for durations comparable to Naᵥ1.4, (Figure 6B–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by coarse-grained simulation data of Naᵥ1.7.

claim: Binding of PIP to the DIV S4–S5 linker to the deactivated VSD-IV in the Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas chimera and resting state model was observed.
source: Binding of PIP to the DIV S4–S5 linker to the deactivated VSD-IV in the Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas chimera and resting state model was also observed (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by coarse-grained simulation data.

claim: In the Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas chimera, the PIP bound at the S4–S5 linker cannot simultaneously associate with the DIII–IV linker due to its sequestration by the CTD.
source: However, in the Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas chimera, the PIP bound at the S4–S5 linker cannot simultaneously associate with the DIII–IV linker (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), due to its sequestration by the CTD, which moves the lysines away from the binding VSD-IV residues (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of simulation data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a greater number of long PIP interactions (>20 µs) with inactivated Naᵥ1.7 compared to Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas or the resting state model where VSD-IV is down.
source: Comparison of binding durations at this site across the three systems reveals a greater number of long PIP interactions (>20 µs) with inactivated Naᵥ1.7 (Dib-Hajj et al., 2013) compared to Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas (Venance et al., 2006) or the resting state model (Mantegazza et al., 2021) where VSD-IV is down, and the DIII–IV linker is dissociated.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by binding duration analysis from simulation data.

claim: There are state-dependent differences in PIP occupancy at the gating charges in each VSD.
source: There are state-dependent differences in PIP occupancy at the gating charges in each VSD (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by occupancy analysis from simulation data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: PIP can associate with the lowest three gating charges VSD-I of the resting state model, but not in the inactivated state.
source: PIP can associate with the lowest three gating charges VSD-I of the resting state model, but not in the inactivated state (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by occupancy analysis from simulation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PIP occupancy is higher at VSD-IV when it is in the deactivated conformation.
source: PIP occupancy is also higher at VSD-IV when it is in the deactivated conformation, however, the presence of a bound CTD as seen in the Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas model reduces this occupancy of PIP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by occupancy analysis from simulation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The presence of a bound CTD reduces PIP occupancy at VSD-IV.
source: PIP occupancy is also higher at VSD-IV when it is in the deactivated conformation, however, the presence of a bound CTD as seen in the Naᵥ1.7-NaᵥPas model reduces this occupancy of PIP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by occupancy analysis from simulation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The PIP binding residues identified are conserved in Naᵥ1.1–1.9.
source: The PIP binding residues identified here are conserved in Naᵥ1.1–1.9 (Figure 5C), suggestive of a shared binding site and mechanism for PIP-mediated modulation across subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The R1642C mutation in Naᵥ1.3 (analogous to R1469 in Naᵥ1.4) leads to developmental epileptic encephalopathy.
source: For example, analogous to the Naᵥ1.4 R1469 residue, the R1642C mutation (in Naᵥ1.3) leads to developmental epileptic encephalopathy (Zaman et al., 2018), and R1644C/H mutations in Naᵥ1.5 (analogous to R1469 in Naᵥ1.4) cause cardiac arrythmias, characterized by accelerated rates of channel recovery from inactivation (Frustaci et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zaman et al., 2018.

claim: R1644C/H mutations in Naᵥ1.5 (analogous to R1469 in Naᵥ1.4) cause cardiac arrythmias, characterized by accelerated rates of channel recovery from inactivation.
source: For example, analogous to the Naᵥ1.4 R1469 residue, the R1642C mutation (in Naᵥ1.3) leads to developmental epileptic encephalopathy (Zaman et al., 2018), and R1644C/H mutations in Naᵥ1.5 (analogous to R1469 in Naᵥ1.4) cause cardiac arrythmias, characterized by accelerated rates of channel recovery from inactivation (Frustaci et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Frustaci et al., 2005.

claim: Mutations at conserved PIP binding residues are likely to reduce PI(4,5)P2 binding, which could be a contributing factor to instability of inactivated state in pathogenic variants.
source: Consistent with our observations, these diseases with mutations on the DIII–IV linker are likely to reduce PI(4,5)P2 binding, which could be a contributing factor to instability of inactivated state in these pathogenic variants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation data and known disease mutations.

claim: The PIP binding site identified harbors sequence and structural similarity to PI(4,5)P2 binding sites found in other cation channels.
source: The PIP binding site identified here harbors sequence and structural similarity to PI(4,5)P2 binding sites found in other cation channels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and sequence comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is resolved at a similar site near the VSD and S4–S5 linker in a cryo-EM structure of Kᵥ7.1, where the phosphate headgroup forms analogous contacts to R249 and R243.
source: For example, PI(4,5)P2 is resolved at a similar site near the VSD and S4–S5 linker in a recent cryo-EM structure of Kᵥ7.1, where the phosphate headgroup forms analogous contacts to R249 and R243 (PDB ID: 6v01) (Sun and MacKinnon, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun and MacKinnon, 2020 and structural comparison.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 binds to the down, deactivated state of VSD-II in Caᵥ2.2.
source: PI(4,5)P2 also binds to the down, deactivated state of VSD-II in Caᵥ2.2 (PDB ID: 7mix) (Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2021.

claim: In Caᵥ2.2, the PI(4,5)P2 headgroup interacts with two VSD-II gating charges, R584 and K587.
source: In this structure, the PI(4,5)P2 headgroup interacts with two VSD-II gating charges, R584 and K587.
evidence: This is structural information from the Caᵥ2.2 structure cited (Gao et al., 2021).

claim: The leftward shift in voltage dependence of inactivation is less pronounced when PI(4,5)P2 is converted to PI(4)P rather than completely dephosphorylated to PI.
source: The leftward shift in voltage dependence of inactivation is less pronounced when PI(4,5)P2 is converted to PI(4)P rather than completely dephosphorylated to PI (Gada et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gada et al., 2023.

claim: PI(4)P may play a compensatory role when PI(4,5)P2 is not present.
source: This suggests that PI(4)P may play a compensatory role when PI(4,5)P2 is not present.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data from Gada et al., 2023.

claim: PI(4)P can stably occupy the identified binding site, albeit with shorter duration and fewer electrostatic interactions compared to PI(4,5)P2.
source: This is supported by our simulations which show that PI(4)P can also stably occupy the identified binding site, albeit with shorter duration and form less electrostatic interactions compared to PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by simulation data comparing PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 binding.

claim: The 5'-phosphate is more important than the 4'-phosphate for forming interactions with the DIV S4–S5 linker residues of the inactivation switch.
source: Our atomistic simulations also showed that the 5'-phosphate is more important than the 4'-phosphate for forming interactions with the DIV S4–S5 linker residues of the inactivation switch.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by interaction analysis from atomistic simulation data.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 binding is preferred over PI(4)P at the identified site.
source: These factors suggest that PI(4,5)P2 binding is preferred over PI(4)P at this site and can better compete to bind over the CTD, implying that PI(4,5)P2 is more effective at stabilizing the inactivated state and inhibiting recovery to the resting state.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation data comparing PI(4,5)P2 and PI(4)P binding.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is more effective at stabilizing the inactivated state and inhibiting recovery to the resting state compared to PI(4)P.
source: These factors suggest that PI(4,5)P2 binding is preferred over PI(4)P at this site and can better compete to bind over the CTD, implying that PI(4,5)P2 is more effective at stabilizing the inactivated state and inhibiting recovery to the resting state.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation data and experimental observations.
